messages.author: 235555c2593ea624
messages.subject: Interactive graphics (in particular maps)
parts:
I started using ggplot about a year ago and really like it.  I have recently been going a lot of map work and am wondering whether I need to use another library to make my choropleths interactive or whether this is something that might be made available in ggplot sometime soon.

My particular case is this: my company sells a product at the zip code level and I can aggregate this data at the county or state level to create maps (and normalize based on census data such as population or median income).   Zip level data is also useful to visualize as a choropleth, but you need a very high zoom level to see the zips.  

Currently I create choropleths for people internally as static images.  I'd like to give them an interactive map where they can zoom in and out and perhaps have the map automatically change level of detail.  Currently I am the bottleneck for visualization, and the US is a big country, so a lot of spatial insight is just not being made (eg show me the zip level sales, by median income, in this region of this state).  There's just too many permutations of the data for me to manually create them all, so it seems like a great candidate for interactive visualization as a choropleth.

I stumbled on this video from 2 years ago where Hadley talks about the future of interactive graphics in R.  My questions are:
  1. What is the state of work of interactive graphics in ggplot?  Is this a project that is under active development? 
  2. If this functionality is not likely to be added to ggplot soon, can people recommend an existing package that contains this functionality?
Thanks.

messages.author: bfc2eb6b71169017
messages.subject: Re: Interactive graphics (in particular maps)
parts:
There's a package called `rCharts` (http://ramnathv.github.io/rCharts/) that offers some interactive stuff via javascript and I think Winston Chang is also working on implementing d3 library.

Cheers,
Roman

messages.author: 4e979d95e92a2b9e
messages.subject: Re: Interactive graphics (in particular maps)
parts:
Or, if your data tables are consistent, you should be able to take what you've done in ggplot, wrap it as a function with parameters for extent or zoom (e.g., state, region, county), facet (income quartiles), and attribute (e.g., monthly or yearly, total sales or sales subset), then write a simple shiny interface to let them pick the parameters in a web app.  That sounds easier than it is, but it isn't too hard.

Tom.
